newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU vets reject ban on suspect animal tissue.
newsitem.headline: EU vets reject ban on suspect animal tissue.

text.p: EU veterinary officials rejected on Tuesday a Commission proposal to ban the use of suspect tissue from sheep and goats, as well as cattle, over the risk of scrapie or mad cow disease, a Commission official said.

The proposal, a precautionary move following British and French research showing that sheep could catch mad cow disease, or Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), will now be discussed by EU farm ministers on December 16-17.
"The officials rejected a slightly amended text," the official said after a meeting of the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior member state veterinary officials.
The proposal, to remove the brains, eyes, spinal cord and spllen from human and animal food, was rejected by 12 member states with only Britain and France voting in support and Ireland abstaining.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, who is due later on Tuesday to appear before the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into BSE, criticised the committee's vote.

"It is unacceptable given the public concern about BSE that some member states refuse to apply all necessary precautions to protect human health and to restore consumer confidence in beef and sheep meat," he said in a statement.

Although the risk is minimal, decision-making bodies must take all necessary action to minimise the risk even further, Fischler said, noting that the Commission's proposal was based on advice from the World Health Organisation and EU veterinary scientists.

The Commission had delayed a vote on the issue when the committee last met on Friday after many member states objected to the proposal, saying the measures were economically unjustified in view of the negligeable risk.
A previous Commission proposal to exclude the suspect tissue from food was rejected by the committee in August.
Sheep have for centuries been known to suffer from scrapie, a brain-wasting disease similar to BSE, which can be passed from one animal to another and from ewe to lamb but not to humans.
